<reason>Both sides built coherent, competitive cases, but CON's central objection—that "social-graph transfer" necessarily means exporting other people's associations without their consent—was never fully neutralized. PRO's mitigation (hashed pointers, reconnect prompts, GDPR-style filtering) was a creative and plausible design, but CON's rebuttal that "the association has already left" once a match is confirmed, and that the prompt itself discloses a relationship, landed as a genuine unresolved gap rather than a strawman. CON also raised an underexploited but damaging point—that mandated interoperability creates an attack surface incumbents can staff but challengers cannot—which cuts against PRO's own pro-competition rationale and was never squarely answered. PRO's strongest closing move, that CON offers no alternative remedy for admitted lock-in, was rhetorically effective but not dispositive, since a negative case opposing a specific legal mandate is not obligated to supply a substitute mechanism; CON explicitly and correctly reframed the burden as "may the law conscript third parties' ties," which is a legitimate way to contest the proposition as written rather than an evasive reframe. CON's sustained "not a suitcase / not portable inventory" framing was also the more memorable and easier throughline for a reader to apply when weighing the clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's rebuttal 1 (B2.3–B2.4), pointing out that PRO's reconnection design still requires a compelled export of "who is tied to whom" before any consent step, and its reinforcement in B4.5 that the prompt itself discloses a prior relationship—never fully defused by PRO's hashed-pointer answer.</best_rebuttal>
